lead: Truth is the thread of today's readings. Paul says that no human failure can make God untrue to his word. Jesus asks his disciples to be so truthful that they need no oath. God's faithfulness comes first, and ours is meant to resemble it. The key words are faithfulness and Yes.

set: Paul has just told his fellow Jews that outward signs without obedience are not enough (2:17–29). The natural question follows: does this leave Israel with nothing? Paul is a Jew himself, and he will not allow that. He writes in the style called diatribe, a teacher's lively argument with an imagined objector, so the questions in this passage are not all his own opinions. Some of them he answers at once, and the longer answer comes in Romans 9–11.
str: vv. 1–2: is there any advantage in being a Jew? Much.
vv. 3–4: human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God's faithfulness.
vv. 5–6: is God then unjust to judge us? By no means.
vv. 7–8: may we do evil for the sake of good? Paul rejects it.
kw: The words God has spoken: the Scriptures and promises entrusted to Israel. The Church has received them from Israel's hands.
One Greek word covers both faith and faithfulness. Paul plays on it: God's pistis is not undone by human apistia.
A strong refusal, literally “may it not be”, which is a favourite of Paul in Romans. It occurs twice in this passage (vv. 4 and 6).
vv: For in the first place the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
Paul says this with pride and gratitude. Later in the letter he adds that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). The Church teaches the same (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).
What if some were unfaithful? Will their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?
Paul says “some”, not all. The question holds for every believer, and for Christians as much as for anyone.
“So that you may be justified in your words, and prevail in your judging.”
Paul quotes Psalm 51:4 in the Greek form, from David's great prayer of repentance. To admit our sin is to say that God is right.
And why not say (as some people slander us by saying that we say), “Let us do evil so that good may come”?
Some people were twisting Paul's preaching of grace into this slogan. He will have none of it.
ch: The Church has made v. 8 a rule of moral life: one may never do evil so that good may result from it (CCC 1756, 1789). It is a sentence for hard decisions, when a wrong act seems to offer a good result. Because God's faithfulness does not wait on ours, the sinner can always come back.

r.h: Let your word be Yes or No
set: This is the fourth of the six “you have heard, but I say” sayings of the Sermon on the Mount (5:21–48). The saying sums up what the Law taught: do not swear falsely, and keep your vows (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21). Jewish tradition itself was uneasy about careless swearing: Sirach warns against getting the habit (Sirach 23:9–11). Jesus takes this concern to its end.
str: vv. 34–36: do not swear at all; four examples.
v. 37: the rule: yes, no, and nothing more.
kw: To break an oath or to swear to something untrue. The Law forbade it, because God's name stood as guarantee.
People sometimes swore by heaven or Jerusalem rather than by God's name, as if this were a lesser thing (compare 23:16–22). Jesus shows that each of these belongs to God.
The Greek could also mean “from evil”, as in the last line of the Our Father (6:13).
vv: But I say to you, Do not swear at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God,
The images come from Isaiah 66:1 (heaven as throne, earth as footstool). You cannot step outside God's presence in order to make a promise on the side.
And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
This is a small and humorous touch. We cannot even control our own hair, so how could we offer it as a pledge?
Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one.
The need for an oath shows how little we trust one another. Jesus wants a community in which a plain word is enough. James repeats the teaching (James 5:12).
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage and explains that the Church's tradition, following St Paul (2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20), has not understood these words as excluding oaths taken for grave and right reasons, such as in court (CCC 2153–2154). St Augustine, commenting on the Sermon on the Mount, says that an oath is not a good thing to seek but may sometimes be needed because of the weakness of those who will not otherwise believe (in substance).

qa: May a Christian take an oath in court?

Yes, for a grave and right reason, as the Catechism says (CCC 2154). St Paul himself calls God to witness. What Jesus forbids is the careless use of God's name, and the double standard in which only a sworn word counts as true.
study: When did I last add “I swear” or something similar because my plain word was not enough? Why was that?
Where has God's faithfulness carried me through my own unfaithfulness?
